lessons.title: Why Starship uses hot staging
lessons.card: Light the engines. Then let go.
lessons.summary: Follow the ignition, venting and separation sequence through an illustrated cutaway of the hot-staging ring.
lessons.answer: Starship ignites its engines before separating from Super Heavy. The vented ring gives the upper stage’s exhaust a route out while the two vehicles are still together.
lessons.intro: Start with the five-stage cutaway, then follow the forces, exhaust flow and vehicle-generation changes below. The drawing represents the earlier vented-ring concept; the article distinguishes that hardware from the integrated V3 hot stage.

stages.title: The booster carries the stack
stages.text: Super Heavy accelerates the combined vehicle. Starship is still attached above the interstage. The enlarged view follows the joint between them.
stages.cold: The stages remain attached during ascent. Both approaches begin with the booster doing the work.

stages.title: Prepare for upper-stage ignition
stages.text: The booster throttles down for staging. The ring between the stages is vented so that exhaust can escape when Starship’s engines ignite.
stages.cold: In this simplified cold-staging comparison, the booster shuts down before separation and upper-stage ignition.

stages.title: Starship ignites
stages.text: The upper-stage engines light while the vehicles are still connected. Exhaust exits through the hot-staging ring. This is the moment the cutaway highlights.
stages.cold: The upper stage separates before lighting its engines. The gap in powered flight is shown as a coast; its duration depends on the rocket.

stages.title: Separate under thrust
stages.text: Starship departs with its engines already running. The booster and ship now have separate jobs: continue the mission above, and prepare the booster’s return below.
stages.cold: After separation and any required settling sequence, the upper-stage engines ignite. The comparison shows a different event order, not a measured performance penalty.

stages.title: Continue on separate paths
stages.text: Starship continues accelerating. Super Heavy turns toward its return sequence. The hot-staging operation has ended; boostback is the next phase.
stages.cold: The upper stage continues its burn. Both methods can work; their hardware, ignition and propellant-management requirements differ.

sections.title: Why the sequence matters
sections.text: A coast creates a pause between powered phases. Igniting before separation reduces that interruption, but introduces a demanding exhaust and separation problem. The ring is part of the hardware that makes that trade possible.

sections.title: What the flight timeline tells us
sections.text: SpaceX’s Flight 14 timeline lists booster MECO at T+2:20 and hot staging at T+2:22. Those are approximate event times for that flight, not universal timings for every Starship vehicle.

misconceptions.title: The exhaust belongs to the upper stage
misconceptions.text: At the hot-staging joint, the key plume comes from Starship’s engines above the booster. The ring vents that exhaust outward.

misconceptions.title: The animation is not a flight simulation
misconceptions.text: The five stages explain the mechanism. Distances, plume shapes and playback speed are schematic; they do not predict a flight’s trajectory or payload gain.

deepDive.title: 1. What “hot” changes: event order

paragraphs.text: A conventional separation can shut down the first stage, release the connection, establish a gap and then ignite the next stage. NASA’s Crew-9 report describes that order for Falcon 9. NASA describes Starship’s upper-stage engines starting before the booster engines have completely cut off and before separation. The word hot describes the powered separation, rather than the atmospheric temperature or the temperature of the rocket’s outer skin.

Three events that look simultaneous in a video remain distinct engineering tasks: starting engines, releasing the structural connection and establishing safe relative motion. Successful ignition alone does not prove separation succeeded. Equally, seeing a gap does not establish that the engines reached their intended operating condition. That is why a useful flight account separates propulsion performance from the separation outcome. This is a way to read the evidence, rather than a claim about SpaceX’s unpublished release logic.

deepDive.title: 2. The performance argument: time and mass

paragraphs.text: The ideal rocket equation relates available velocity change to effective exhaust velocity and the logarithm of the initial-to-final mass ratio: Δv = ve × ln(m0 / mf). It explains why carrying additional structure has a performance cost. It does not, by itself, calculate the payload benefit of changing a staging sequence; a real ascent also has gravity, drag, steering and mission constraints.

During an unpowered interval the rocket still moves, and may still gain altitude. It is not suspended in place. In a simplified vertical coast with constant local gravity and negligible drag, its upward speed changes by −g × Δt. Taking an explicitly assumed g = 9.8 m/s², a two-second interval changes upward speed by approximately −19.6 m/s. This is an illustrative calculation, not a measured Starship loss or a prediction of payload gain.

Continuing thrust through staging addresses that interruption. It also changes the hardware the vehicle must carry and the loads the separation must withstand. The right comparison is a complete trajectory and mass budget. A claim such as “this adds a fixed number of tonnes” needs that supporting analysis, with the vehicle version and mission held constant; it cannot be read directly from the cutaway.

deepDive.title: 3. The hard part is the plume

paragraphs.text: NASA’s 2024 analysis describes upper-stage exhaust impinging on the booster shield inside a confined interstage. At the low ambient pressure of separation, the plume expands around the vehicle. The problem includes pressure loads as well as heating; a vent does not make those interactions disappear. NASA compared different geometries and engine-start sequences, including moving-body simulations, and reported favourable agreement with second-flight data.

Think of three questions when viewing the enlarged joint: where can gas leave, which surfaces can it strike, and how do the two vehicles move while that flow is changing? The red arrows show the intended exhaust route in the schematic. They are not a map of Mach number, heat flux or pressure. Turning an explanation into a credible prediction would require boundary conditions, material properties, mesh resolution and validation against measurements.

deepDive.title: 4. Thrust does not need something to push against

paragraphs.text: A rocket accelerates by expelling mass. The thrust equation includes exhaust momentum and the difference between nozzle-exit and surrounding pressure. Starship’s engines do not need to push on the booster to function. During hot staging, however, exhaust also strikes nearby structure, so the overall interaction contains more than the free-flight thrust of an isolated engine.

This distinction helps explain the drawing: the upper stage’s thrust accelerates that stage, while plume interaction imposes additional loads on the connected system. Once released, relative acceleration opens the gap. The visual model leaves out engine transients, structural vibration and propellant motion. Those omissions are useful for learning the sequence, but they are exactly the details a separation qualification programme has to investigate.

deepDive.title: 5. The hardware changed: earlier ring versus V3

paragraphs.text: SpaceX’s V3 introduction describes an integrated hot stage replacing the previous single-use protective interstage. The forward dome of the booster fuel tank is exposed to the upper-stage exhaust, with internal tank pressure and a non-structural steel layer providing protection. This is a vehicle-generation change, not simply the old ring with a different label.

Read historical images with their flight and vehicle version attached. A detached interstage seen on an earlier flight does not establish that every later booster carries and discards the same part. The cutaway above teaches the earlier vented-ring concept. The table makes its scope explicit rather than silently presenting one geometry as the permanent design.

deepDive.title: 6. How to read the flight timeline

paragraphs.text: SpaceX’s Flight 14 timeline places most-engine cutoff at T+2:20, hot staging at T+2:22 and boostback start at T+2:27. The five-second difference between the last two listed events is arithmetic from approximate published times. It does not identify the exact instant a mechanical latch opened, or the duration of every engine transient.

A useful review records the vehicle generation, mission objective, engine-start outcome, separation outcome and booster-return outcome separately. A later failure should not erase an earlier demonstrated event; an earlier success should not certify every later event. When new footage arrives, compare like with like: the same camera angle, a reliable clock, and the mission’s own event descriptions. Keep launch schedules and future catch targets in the maintained tracker, where they can be updated without rewriting this engineering guide.

faq.title: Does cold staging mean the rocket stops moving?
faq.text: No. It coasts. Its velocity changes under gravity and aerodynamic forces while propulsion is interrupted. The key difference is the order of separation and ignition.

faq.title: Why is there no exact payload gain here?
faq.text: A payload comparison needs a specified vehicle, mission trajectory, structural mass and propulsion assumptions. The ideal rocket equation alone cannot supply a defensible Starship-specific number.

faq.title: Is the illustrated ring the current V3 configuration?
faq.text: The main drawing represents the earlier vented-ring concept. The V3 comparison explains the integrated hot-stage change using SpaceX’s dated description.

lessons.title: How a booster catch works
lessons.card: A landing pad that reaches out.
lessons.summary: See the return, alignment and transfer of load to the tower, with elevation and overhead views.
lessons.answer: The returning booster slows and aligns with the tower so its catch fittings can meet the arms. Once supported, the booster’s weight is carried by the tower rather than landing legs.
lessons.intro: The catch is the final step in a return-to-launch-site sequence. Start with the elevation and overhead animation, then examine braking, alignment, the structural load path and the distinction between one successful recovery and repeatable reuse.

stages.title: Return toward the launch site
stages.text: After separation, the booster’s return sequence brings it back toward the launch area. This diagram begins with the approach; it does not plot the full boostback trajectory.

stages.title: Control the approach
stages.text: The booster must reach the catch area with the required position and orientation. Compare the elevation with the overhead view: arriving at the right height alone is not enough.

stages.title: Slow for the catch
stages.text: The landing burn reduces the booster’s speed as it approaches the arms. The illustrated flame marks that phase, without assigning an engine count or a fixed burn duration.

stages.title: Meet the catch fittings
stages.text: The booster’s catch fittings and the arms must line up. The red markers identify the relationship being explained, not the tolerances of an actual flight.

stages.title: The tower carries the load
stages.text: Once supported by the arms, the booster hangs at the tower. The final view highlights the support path and turns off the landing-burn illustration.

sections.title: Why put the landing hardware on the ground?
sections.text: A tower catch moves some recovery infrastructure off the flying vehicle. It also makes the return depend on a particular facility and a tightly coordinated approach. That is the central engineering trade.

sections.title: A demonstrated milestone
sections.text: SpaceX’s fifth Starship flight demonstrated the first Super Heavy tower catch. The official film below is the reference for the broad sequence; the illustration is an explanation of that sequence, not a reconstruction of its telemetry.

misconceptions.title: The arms are not a net
misconceptions.text: The mechanism depends on alignment with the booster’s catch area. A diagram of two arms around a cylinder is not a description of the complete guidance and control system.

misconceptions.title: A booster catch does not prove a ship catch
misconceptions.text: Starship and Super Heavy are different vehicles. A completed booster catch should not be presented as confirmation of a future ship catch or an unannounced flight plan.

deepDive.title: 1. Returning is a trajectory problem

paragraphs.text: After staging, the booster is both high above Earth and moving away from the launch site. Returning requires changing its trajectory, not simply turning its nose upward. A boostback burn changes velocity so that the later descent can approach the launch area; a landing burn addresses the final approach. Those are different jobs, even though both use rocket propulsion. SpaceX’s Flight 5 sequence includes separation, boostback, coast and the final landing burn before capture.

A useful mental model separates position from velocity. Two boosters can occupy the same point and need completely different control actions if one is descending quickly and the other is nearly stationary. The same applies laterally: being beside the tower is insufficient if sideways motion is still carrying the vehicle away. Our diagram shows positions at five explanatory stages, not the full six-dimensional flight state or its estimated uncertainty.

deepDive.title: 2. Why the landing burn must beat gravity

paragraphs.text: Consider a simplified vertical free-body model during a powered descent. Let upward be positive, T be the upward thrust, m the instantaneous vehicle mass and g local gravity. Ignoring aerodynamic force, vertical acceleration is a = T/m − g. To reduce a downward speed, acceleration must point upward: thrust greater than weight is needed during that braking interval. Merely balancing weight would preserve the existing downward velocity in this simplified model.

The formula is an instantaneous relationship. Propellant consumption changes mass, engines have transients and a tilted vehicle directs some thrust sideways. A full return model also includes atmospheric forces. The graphic therefore shows the existence of the braking phase without inventing a throttle curve or a catch-speed specification. It also avoids the misleading picture of a booster simply dropping into waiting arms at high speed.

math.title: A catch is about removing motion before support
terms: g: local gravitational acceleration, in m/s²
math.note: Simplified vertical force balance; no aerodynamic force. It does not supply Super Heavy’s mass, thrust schedule or catch velocity.

deepDive.title: 3. Alignment has several dimensions

paragraphs.text: Height is one coordinate. The catch also depends on lateral position, attitude and the orientation of the catch interface relative to the arms. The overhead view exists because a side-on video can hide an offset toward or away from the camera. Likewise, a small angular error at one location can create a larger offset elsewhere on a long structure. This is general rigid-body geometry, not a disclosure of SpaceX’s guidance algorithm.

For small angles measured in radians, lateral offset is approximately length × angle. As a purely hypothetical example, a point 10 metres from a rotation centre moves about 0.175 metres sideways for a one-degree rotation: 10 × π/180. Neither input is a published catch tolerance. The calculation explains why orientation and position belong in the same discussion; it must not be repackaged as the accuracy of a real flight.

deepDive.title: 4. From engine support to structural support

paragraphs.text: Before capture, aerodynamic and propulsive forces act on the flying vehicle. After a supported catch, its weight has a structural route through the catch interface, arms and tower to the ground. The engine flame disappearing is only one visible part of that transition. The important mechanical question is where the load is carried and how relative motion is reduced during contact.

In a simplified model, changing momentum by Δp over a time Δt requires an average net force Δp/Δt. For the same mass and residual approach speed, a shorter arrest time implies a greater average net decelerating force. The actual contact forces also depend on weight, geometry and compliance. This is why an illustration cannot certify arm loads from the size of a flame or a single video frame.

A tower catch moves recovery hardware and some of its maintenance burden onto the launch site. That may reduce what the booster has to carry, but it adds constraints on the facility, approach corridor and availability of the catch system. The trade is not “free landing mass”; it is a different allocation of mass, infrastructure and operational risk.

deepDive.title: 5. Catch interfaces evolve with the booster

paragraphs.text: SpaceX’s V3 announcement describes three grid fins rather than four, each enlarged by 50%, with revised positioning and new catch points. The same update describes lowering the fins to reduce hot-staging heat exposure. That links ascent separation, aerodynamic control and recovery hardware in a single design change.

Do not treat every protrusion in historical footage as the same permanent catch fitting. Identify the booster generation and the dated source before discussing a specific interface. The animation explains approach and support using earlier geometry. It does not certify the attachment detail, contact surface or actuator arrangement of every later vehicle. A sharper photograph cannot supply a structural specification by itself.

deepDive.title: 6. A catch, a recovery and reuse are different milestones

paragraphs.text: Flight 5 established that a Super Heavy booster could return to the tower and be caught. A successful catch is evidence for that event. Demonstrating repeatable reuse requires additional evidence: inspection, condition of hardware, work performed between flights and subsequent flight outcomes. The words recovered, reused and rapidly reused should therefore be attached to different observations.

A mission can also separate upper-stage and booster results. The booster returns early while the ship continues its own mission. Conversely, a booster catch cannot establish that the ship has been caught, or that a later announced objective has already happened. Those distinctions make the tracker more valuable: it records demonstrated outcomes alongside the vehicle and date rather than letting one spectacular image stand in for an entire programme.

When analysing the next catch, record the mission, booster generation, whether the catch was attempted, whether support was achieved and whether later reuse was demonstrated. If a source gives only an approximate event time, retain that uncertainty. Avoid converting a broadcast clock or a slow-motion replay into an engineering tolerance. The lesson explains the system; the mission record supplies the outcome.

faq.title: Do the arms absorb the full energy of a falling booster?
faq.text: The landing burn removes most of the motion before support. Residual motion and contact loads still matter, but this is not a free-fall impact into a stationary net.

faq.title: Why does the diagram use two views?
faq.text: A side view shows height but can hide lateral offset. A plan view exposes a different part of the alignment problem. Neither view contains the whole flight state.

faq.title: Does a catch mean the booster can immediately fly again?
faq.text: No. Recovery, inspection, refurbishment, reflight and rapid turnaround require separate evidence. A catch demonstrates one part of that chain.

lessons.title: Why FSD differs between cars
lessons.summary: Untangle the three things that determine a car’s feature set, then compare the tracker’s reported software branches.
lessons.answer: An FSD label does not describe every Tesla’s capabilities. Hardware, installed software, vehicle configuration and regional availability all matter. Full Self-Driving (Supervised) still requires an attentive driver.

stages.title: Start with the vehicle
stages.text: A model name alone does not identify its complete configuration. Build date, equipment and the information shown in the vehicle are better starting points than another owner’s video.

stages.title: Identify the hardware
stages.text: Hardware generations describe the vehicle’s computing and camera configuration. A newer software announcement should not be read as a promise that every hardware generation receives the same features.

stages.title: Check the installed software
stages.text: The vehicle software build and the FSD version are different labels. Record both when comparing release notes. A reported build in a sample is not confirmation that your car has received it.

stages.title: Check the region and entitlement
stages.text: Tesla says availability can depend on configuration, hardware, software, region, model and model year. A release in one market does not establish availability in another.

stages.title: Keep the driver in the loop
stages.text: Tesla describes these features as supervised driver assistance. They do not replace the driver or make the consumer vehicle autonomous. Review the instructions for your particular car.

sections.title: Read a version comparison correctly
sections.text: The table separates hardware, FSD version and vehicle build. Different values are highlighted so you can see what actually changed. It reports the site tracker’s snapshot; it does not certify eligibility for a particular VIN.

sections.title: Use your car as the final check
sections.text: The useful question is what is installed, enabled and supported on your vehicle. Use its software screen, release notes and owner’s manual alongside the tracker. The diagram deliberately makes no claim about Tesla’s internal neural-network design.

misconceptions.title: A shared name does not mean a shared release
misconceptions.text: Two cars can show the FSD brand while running different software branches or having different supported features.

misconceptions.title: Supervised is a meaningful requirement
misconceptions.text: The driver must remain attentive. A polished route demonstration does not establish that a consumer car can operate without supervision.

deepDive.title: 1. From camera images to vehicle control

paragraphs.text: Tesla’s Model Y manual describes cameras around the vehicle feeding a model of the surrounding area. It says the installed AI computer processes neural networks and makes driving decisions. Those are the documented ingredients. The three-layer diagram above separates hardware, installed software and regional availability; it is not a schematic of the proprietary network layers or a claim about how many networks a given release contains.

As a general engineering model, an assisted-driving system must connect sensing to a representation of the scene, a choice of motion and commands to the vehicle. Errors can arise at each boundary: an object may be obscured, its motion may be uncertain, or a planned manoeuvre may become unsuitable as traffic changes. This model helps explain limitations without pretending Tesla has published a fixed perception/planning/control architecture for every release.

deepDive.title: 2. Hardware is a physical configuration

paragraphs.text: Identify the installed computer through the touchscreen rather than relying on model year or the appearance of a camera lens. Tesla’s support instructions point to Controls, Software and Additional Vehicle Information. Its computer-upgrade page describes a particular 2.0/2.5-to-3.0 programme; that is not documentation of universal eligibility for a different retrofit. Hardware labels in the tracker should be read alongside the vehicle’s own configuration.

The engineering reason hardware matters is that running a model has finite memory, computing, thermal and input/output requirements. A software update can change what is computed, but it does not physically add a new camera or replace a processor. That general constraint does not establish which future Tesla release can run on which vehicle. Claims about memory bandwidth, chip performance or upgrade dates need a specific primary specification or dated announcement; a hardware number is not enough to infer them.

deepDive.title: 3. Build numbers are not capability scores

paragraphs.text: A vehicle build identifies an installed software package. An FSD version identifies a driving-software release. Trackers may report both, along with hardware and market. Treat the values as labels to match with release notes, rather than decimal numbers: a version string is not a measurement of intelligence, and a larger-looking suffix does not prove that every feature is newer or available on every branch.

A useful comparison keeps five fields together: computer hardware, vehicle build, FSD version, entitlement and region. If one is missing, say so. The table in this lesson shows reported branches from the maintained tracker; it deliberately does not invent a yes/no capability matrix from version names. Its snapshot date records the data, while the reference-review date records when the explanation was checked.

deepDive.title: 4. A rollout is a distribution process

paragraphs.text: Tesla says updates arrive on a rolling basis. Two apparently similar cars can therefore be on different builds at the same time. Advanced requests updates as they become available for that configuration and region; it is not a promise of immediate access to every new release. A tracker’s first observation establishes that a sample received a build, not that an entire fleet is eligible.

Download and installation are separate states. The Model Y manual says software can download before installation, and the car cannot be driven while installation is taking place. It also says Advanced does not enrol the vehicle in the early-access programme. After installation, read the release notes on the car: they describe that installed package and may contain feature-specific instructions.

This explains a common apparent contradiction: a website can correctly report a release while your car correctly reports that it is up to date. Those statements concern different scopes. The useful next step is to identify the installed build and review official availability information, rather than treating a sample count or an enthusiastic owner post as an update guarantee.

deepDive.title: 5. Calibration and visibility are part of the system

paragraphs.text: The cited US Model Y chapter lists a front-bumper camera, a rear camera, one in each door pillar, two at the windshield and one on each front fender: eight road-facing cameras in that configuration. The cabin camera is separate. This inventory belongs to that manual, rather than every Tesla carrying an HW4 label.

The US Model Y camera chapter gives a typical calibration distance of 20–25 miles, or 32–40 kilometres, while noting that conditions change the result. It describes calibration as necessary before certain assistance and active-safety functions can first become available, and after some service work. A progress indicator is evidence about calibration status; it is not a general confidence score for every future driving situation.

Visibility matters after calibration too. The manual identifies obstructions and environmental conditions as performance limits. A clear lens cannot reveal something hidden behind another vehicle, and an illustration of a camera cone is not a certified coverage envelope. Separate a dirty or blocked camera, incomplete calibration and an ambiguous traffic scene when diagnosing a limitation: they describe different causes, even if the driver ultimately has to take over.

The cabin-facing camera has a different job from road-facing cameras. Tesla’s FSD chapter describes it monitoring driver attentiveness while supervised driving is engaged. Watching the driver does not remove the driver’s responsibility to watch the road. Use the manual for the exact configuration and region; assistance naming and available controls can change with software.

deepDive.title: 6. What a driving demonstration can prove

paragraphs.text: A route video can document one journey under particular conditions. It does not, without a denominator and a test protocol, establish the probability of a safe outcome across weather, road layouts and interventions. To compare two demonstrations, ask whether the route, traffic, driver input, hardware, software and editing are comparable. A montage of smooth turns is different evidence from an independently specified test.

NHTSA distinguishes momentary warnings/interventions from continuous assistance. A system that performs steering and speed control while the human remains responsible belongs to a different category from a vehicle that can operate without that human role. Tesla’s consumer FSD support material continues to require active supervision. Automation terminology should describe the responsibility and operating conditions, not how impressive a single manoeuvre looks.

For a feature claim, prefer the car’s release notes and manual, then a dated official announcement with its hardware and region. Owner reports are useful observations when labelled as such. They can establish that a particular owner reported an event; they cannot automatically establish a universal rollout, an internal design detail or a future upgrade commitment. This is why the lesson connects to the live tracker instead of freezing a list of promises into the artwork.

faq.title: Does Advanced make the car eligible for every FSD release?
faq.text: No. It affects update preference for releases ready for the vehicle. Configuration, region and other eligibility conditions still apply, and Advanced is not Tesla’s early-access programme.

faq.title: Can the same vehicle build contain different available features?
faq.text: A build label alone does not describe hardware, entitlement or regional availability. Compare all five fields and the car’s release notes.

faq.title: Why not publish processor-performance ratios here?
faq.text: A defensible ratio needs a specified metric, workload, hardware and primary source. Peak compute figures, memory bandwidth and real driving capability are different measurements.

stages.title: A warning may be issued
stages.text: Tesla describes Forward Collision Warning as a visual and audible alert. That warning is distinct from a braking command. The driver remains responsible for responding.

stages.title: Braking assistance may intervene

stages.title: The driver remains responsible

sections.title: Keep the feature names separate
sections.text: An emergency-braking feature is not proof that FSD will engage or re-engage. For a release carrying a Collision Evasion label, check its exact notes, supported hardware and region in the current software tracker.

sections.title: Why this diagram has no success score
sections.text: A successful-looking animation cannot establish real-world avoidance performance. This sequence teaches the distinction between a hazard, a warning and a possible intervention. It is not an instruction to test the system.

misconceptions.title: A warning does not promise braking

misconceptions.title: A demonstration does not establish availability

deepDive.title: 1. Three different kinds of intervention

paragraphs.text: A warning informs the driver. Braking assistance changes vehicle speed. Steering assistance changes the path. NHTSA distinguishes these functions even when several appear in the same car. A dashboard message, a brake-pedal movement and a steering input are therefore different evidence. Recording which occurred is more useful than calling every response “self-driving”.

Tesla’s Collision Avoidance Assist chapter separately describes Forward Collision Warning, Automatic Emergency Braking and Obstacle-Aware Acceleration. The last can reduce acceleration near a detected obstacle; it is not interchangeable with emergency braking. The same chapter’s approximate 5–200 km/h FCW/AEB operating range belongs to the specified US Model Y manual. It is not a guarantee for every model, direction of travel, software release or road condition.

headers: What that alone does not establish

deepDive.title: 2. Closing speed is different from road speed

paragraphs.text: Suppose two vehicles are travelling in the same direction. In a simplified constant-speed model, closing speed is the following vehicle’s speed minus the lead vehicle’s speed. If a follower is at 60 km/h and the vehicle ahead is at 40 km/h, the gap is shrinking at 20 km/h, or about 5.56 m/s. With a 20-metre gap, the constant-speed time to contact is about 3.6 seconds. These are hypothetical inputs, not a detection or activation threshold.

Change the lead vehicle to a stationary object and the same follower closes at 16.67 m/s. At a 20-metre gap, the constant-speed time becomes about 1.2 seconds. Neither number predicts what a particular assistance system will do. Braking by either vehicle, a cut-in or a curved path changes the calculation. This is why a single speedometer reading cannot describe the complete collision problem.

Time to contact is a model, not a certainty. It depends on the assumption that relative motion continues as estimated. A real system must also decide whether an object is in the relevant path, whether its motion estimate is reliable and what intervention is appropriate. That conceptual chain explains why detecting something in an image and deciding to brake are separate tasks.

deepDive.title: 3. Delay and braking consume different distances

paragraphs.text: Stopping distance includes travel before braking begins and travel while speed is being reduced. Rhode Island’s driver guidance separates perception, reaction and braking, and notes that traction changes braking distance. Assistance may change parts of the response, but it does not remove the physical distance required to slow the vehicle.

For an educational constant-deceleration model, distance = v × t + v²/(2a). Here v is initial speed in m/s, t an assumed delay in seconds and a a positive constant braking deceleration in m/s². The first term grows directly with speed; the second grows with its square. Doubling speed therefore doubles the delay distance and quadruples the braking distance when the assumptions stay the same.

The chart assumes a one-second delay and 6 m/s² constant deceleration on a straight, level path. It omits tyre variation, grade, brake build-up, changing friction and a moving target. At 60 km/h, delay travel is 16.7 metres and modelled braking travel is 23.1 metres, totalling 39.8 metres. These are arithmetic results from chosen inputs, not measured Tesla stopping distances, safe following gaps or AEB performance specifications.

math.title: An assumption-led calculation
terms: v = speed ÷ 3.6, converting km/h to m/s
math.note: Educational model only. A real collision-assistance system has different, situation-dependent timing and braking. Do not use the result to plan a following distance or test the car.

deepDive.title: 4. What independent crash research actually found

paragraphs.text: Jessica Cicchino’s 2017 IIHS study compared police-reported crashes in 22 US states during 2010–2014. It estimated rear-end striking-crash reductions of 27% for forward collision warning alone, 43% for low-speed AEB and 50% for warning with AEB. The corresponding injury-crash reductions were 20%, 45% and 56%. These describe the studied systems and populations, not Tesla’s current FSD or a Collision Evasion release.

Those percentages are relative reductions in crash-involvement rates, not a guarantee that an individual intervention succeeds. The population, exposure measure, comparison group and crash definition matter. A result for rear-end crashes should not be relabelled as a result for all crashes, pedestrian incidents or autonomous driving.

A 2019 IIHS study examined the rear-end crashes that remained. Turning, lane-changing lead vehicles, unusual vehicle types, snowy/icy roads and higher-speed roads were among the circumstances overrepresented in crashes involving AEB-equipped striking vehicles. The finding motivates broader testing. It does not imply AEB causes every crash in those circumstances or gives an individual Tesla a numerical failure probability.

deepDive.title: 5. Why false alerts and missed hazards both matter

paragraphs.text: A system must act on incomplete observations while the scene changes. Triggering too readily can create unwanted interventions; triggering too late can leave less distance to respond. This is a general detection-and-control trade-off, not a claim about Tesla’s internal confidence thresholds. A chart of visible camera coverage would not solve it: seeing an object does not establish its future path or whether an intervention is appropriate.

The Model Y camera chapter identifies obstructions and visibility conditions as performance concerns. Clean lenses and calibration address prerequisites, not every ambiguity. Separate sensing from stopping physics: better braking cannot compensate for every missed observation.

A useful incident record includes the vehicle, installed build, feature settings, conditions, displayed message and available unedited footage. Avoid guessing whether a visible slowing was a driver input or an automated action. Without the relevant evidence, an honest account can describe the observation while leaving the mechanism unresolved.

deepDive.title: 6. Where release-specific Collision Evasion fits

paragraphs.text: The label Collision Evasion should be tied to the exact software release and its own description. It must not inherit every property of FCW, AEB or supervised driving merely because those functions share a vehicle. Likewise, the absence of that label in one public manual is not proof that no release contains additional behaviour. The correct question is which documented behaviour applies to which configuration.

For an automatic-engagement claim, look for the release identifier, supported hardware, market, prerequisites, operating conditions and instructions for driver control. A social clip can be an observation; a complete primary release note is stronger evidence for the intended feature conditions. This review did not establish an accessible exact primary release note covering every re-engagement claim, so the guide does not turn secondary descriptions into operating instructions.

Use the linked software tracker for current reports, then confirm the installed car’s own release notes and manual. A comprehensive explanation should make uncertainty specific: what is documented, what is calculated and what remains unverified. It should neither promise a rescue manoeuvre nor dismiss a reported feature simply because the name resembles an older safety function.

faq.title: Does the IIHS 50% result measure Tesla’s Collision Evasion?
faq.text: No. It is a historical estimate for rear-end striking crashes among systems and vehicles in the 2017 study. It is not a Tesla-specific score or a current software evaluation.

faq.title: Does an operating-speed range guarantee intervention?
faq.text: No. A listed range is one operating condition. It does not guarantee detection, braking, avoidance or applicability to another model or market.

faq.title: Why use a hypothetical stopping model?
faq.text: It isolates how delay and speed affect distance. Its assumptions are shown so readers can understand the arithmetic without mistaking the result for a vehicle test.
